sources.citation: Pennington, Ryan. 2016. A grammar of Ma Manda, a Papuan language of Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea. PhD thesis, James Cook University.
sources.note: Most thorough modern description of an Erap language (Ma Manda, mama1271); its introduction surveys the Erap family and may contain comparative remarks on Nema, and its stress chapter is the nearest family-internal reference point. Not a Gusan source.

sources.citation: Retsema, Thom, Margaret Potter & Rachel Gray. 2009. Mungkip: an endangered language. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2009-015. Dallas: SIL International.
sources.note: Only published work naming Nema; a sociolinguistic survey of neighbouring Mungkip with comparative wordlists that may include Nema forms with phonetic transcription. Unlikely to state a stress rule but should be checked.
Classification Erap > Finungwan-Mamaa-Gusan; alternate name Nema; only reference shown is Hooley & McElhanon 1970. No descriptive source listed.
Stub; cites Ethnologue 18th ed. and Retsema, Potter & Gray 2009 (SIL Electronic Survey Report 2009-015) for the name Nema. No phonology.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority (submitted by Chris Rice, SIL-PNG). 2015. Change Request 2015-039: add name 'Nema' for [gsn].
sources.note: Name-change request only: speakers in Kokosan, Gom, Damet, Finongan call the language Nema; cites Retsema, Potter & Gray 2009 (SIL ESR 2009-015). No phonology.

sources.citation: Hammarström, Harald & Sebastian Nordhoff. 2012. Online appendix to 'The languages of Melanesia: quantifying the level of coverage'. In N. Evans & M. Klamer (eds), Melanesian languages on the edge of Asia (LD&C Special Publication 5), 13-34. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: coverage inventory only: entry lists Claassen & McElhanon 1970, Ross 1995, Smith 1988 only; no stress/tone statement (database of descriptive coverage, not a description)
sources.venue: Melanesian languages on the edge of Asia (LD&C Special Publication 5)

sources.citation: Smith, Geoffrey P. 1988. Morobe counting systems. In Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 26 (Pacific Linguistics A-76), 1-132. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.note: No phonology content: Gusan numerals from village informants in broad transcription (1 kobogen, 2 yare, 3 yare kuboc, 4 yarewo yarewo / imaninamo, 5 iman, 6 kaiwi kuboc, 10 kuman ta), classified as a type C (two numeral words + hand tally) system; author states a narrow phonetic transcription 'was not considered to be essential' and uses a schwa symbol for 'an unaccented neutral vowel' generically. No stress marks, no stress or tone statement.
sources.venue: Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 26 (Pacific Linguistics A-76)

sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. 1984. A linguistic field guide to the Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics D-57.
sources.note: Village list only: (64) Gusan pop. 869, villages Boiran, Borin, Gom, Gusan, Nandalamen. No phonology, no stress.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1975. North-Eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1: Papuan languages and the New Guinea linguistic scene (Pacific Linguistics C-38), 527-567. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.note: Village/population entry for Gusan and the family-level phoneme table only; no occurrence of stress, accent, tone or pitch in the chapter.
sources.venue: New Guinea area languages and language study

sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. & C. L. Voorhoeve. 1970/1973. The Trans-New Guinea Phylum: explorations in deep-level genetic relationships. Pacific Linguistics B-16.
sources.note: Source of the only Gusan wordlist in circulation (ASJP, TransNewGuinea.org); comparative wordlist, no stress marking expected.

sources.citation: Claassen, Oren R. & Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Finisterre Range - New Guinea. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 11 (Pacific Linguistics A-23), 45-78. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Gusan entry (2.7.3, p. 56) is a one-paragraph lexicostatistical/survey note (pop. 800, some dialectal variation). Section 6.1 gives phonological sketches of Rawa, Suroi, Wantoat, Uri, Uruwa languages etc., not Gusan. The only stress remark (p. 66) reads: "Stress is phonemic in Rawa but probably sub-phonemic in Yupna and Wantoat. In none of these languages does it carry a heavy functional load." Nothing on Gusan stress.
sources.venue: Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 11 (Pacific Linguistics A-23)

sources.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. & Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Morobe District - New Guinea. In Wurm & Laycock (eds), Pacific Linguistic Studies in Honour of Arthur Capell (Pacific Linguistics C-13), 1065-1094.
sources.note: Lexicostatistical survey only (Gusan 35% with Nimi, 40% with Irumu, 30% with Sakam; pop. 800, village list). No phonology, no stress.
sources.venue: Pacific Linguistic Studies in Honour of Arthur Capell (Pacific Linguistics C-13)

sources.note: 56 lexical items, all from McElhanon & Voorhoeve (1970/1973) comparative wordlist; no phonological description.

sources.note: Per Pennington 2013 (fn. 11) it is 'a large sociolinguistic survey report' that 'includes phonological and dialect observations' and 170-item IPA wordlists for three Nema villages (plus Ma Manda and Sama); SIL-PNG survey reports of this period usually carry a short phonology note that may remark on stress or the absence/presence of tone; Pennington, who used it, reports that no Erap language has been analyzed as tonal. It is the only first-hand phonetic material on Nema known to exist.
